newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso says he will fight for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso says he will fight for reforms.

text.p: In a bid for support in a crucial reform vote later this week, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said on Monday he would not give up his drive to streamline Brazil.
In an interview with Globo television, excerpts of which were shown in a newscast, Cardoso also said he was considering shutting ministries to cut spending.
"The reforms are essential and I will fight for them until the very end," the president said, defying critics who say his government's reform program has run out of steam.
He called on the Chambers of Deputies to defeat an opposition amendment to the government's civil service reform bill, which would allow civil servants to keep their lifetime job guarantees.

"Let me tell you what's being voted on Wednesday," Cardoso said. "It's a rule that will allow public workers...to be dismissed even if they are found to be incompetent. That's an item of public morality. Whoever votes against that is saying that incompetent people can stay in their jobs for life."

Government-allied lawmakers and officials have recently begun to concede that the civil service reform, and another bill aimed at modernizing the pensions system, may not be approved before elections in October 1998.

The bills, sent to Congress two years ago, are considered essential to the long-term prospects of the economic plan introduced by Cardoso while finance minister in 1994 and which continues to keep inflation below ten percent a year.
But they have run into stiff opposition in parliament where many lawmakers are closely linked to Brazil's powerful civil service.

The president, considered favorite to win next year's presidential elections, also said he was considering the possibility of axing some ministries, citing the mines and energy ministry and the transport ministry. A Globo interviewer also mentioned the communications ministry.
"What do we need all these ministries for?" Cardoso asked. "We could make do with just one to take care of the government and the rest could be given to agencies.

Asked whether he might have done anything differently with hindsight, the president said: "I would have placed less emphasis on the idea that it was reforms or nothing. People have the idea the government is tied to Congress."
He also said he regretted not "making changes in the foreign exchange area" while finance minister.

The president ruled out the possibility of his government privatizing oil giant Petrobras and state bank Banco do Brasil. He also said a study by a government accounting agency, which detected cuts in real terms in spending on social services during his term, was wrong.
